title: The Friend of God at Mamre
summary: The LORD visits Abraham’s tent, renews the promise of Isaac to doubting Sarah, and reveals Sodom’s judgment to the patriarch who intercedes for it.
historicalContext: The scene belongs to the last year before Isaac’s birth, soon after the covenant of circumcision in chapter 17. Abraham is ninety-nine, Sarah eighty-nine, and they live as tent-dwelling sojourners among the great trees of Mamre near Hebron, where Abraham had built an altar. Hospitality in that world was a sacred duty: a traveller crossing open country depended on the kindness of strangers for water, shade, and food, and a host’s honour was measured by the generosity of his welcome. Below the hill country lay the well-watered cities of the plain, Sodom and Gomorrah, prosperous and notorious, which Lot had chosen as his home and which Abraham had once rescued from the eastern kings. The chapter therefore stands at the meeting point of two worlds: the household of promise in the hills and the urban culture of the valley, whose wickedness had already been named in 13:13.
literaryContext: Chapter 18 opens the third scene in the Abraham narrative where God’s promise of a son and God’s judgment of the nations are held side by side. Its first half (vv. 1–15) is an annunciation story, building on the promise to Abraham in 17:15–21 and now bringing Sarah herself into hearing. Its second half (vv. 16–33) moves from a meal to a conversation, as the LORD shares his counsel with Abraham and the patriarch pleads for Sodom. The chapter is carefully paired with chapter 19: Abraham sits at his tent door at noon, Lot sits in the city gate at evening; Abraham runs and lavishes a feast, Lot must press reluctant guests and offers unleavened bread. Key words bind the whole together: “see,” “laugh,” “righteous,” “cry,” and “Lord.” The contrast between the righteousness Abraham is to teach and the outcry rising from Sodom frames the theology of the chapter.
themes: God’s condescending fellowship with his friend
Hospitality that welcomes the divine guest
Nothing too wonderful for the LORD
Grace that corrects and restores doubting faith
The Judge of all the earth acting justly
Bold, humble intercession for the lost

outline.title: The Divine Guests at Abraham’s Tent
outline.summary: The LORD and two companions arrive at noon, and Abraham hurries to provide water, rest, and a lavish meal that his guests accept.

outline.title: The Promise and Sarah’s Laughter
outline.summary: The LORD fixes the time of Isaac’s birth, exposes Sarah’s hidden laughter, and answers her doubt with his own unlimited power.

outline.title: The LORD Confides His Purpose
outline.summary: As the visitors look toward Sodom, the LORD resolves to share his plan with Abraham, whose calling is to teach righteousness and justice.

outline.title: Abraham Pleads for Sodom
outline.summary: Standing before the LORD, Abraham appeals to divine justice and mercy, and God agrees to spare the city for as few as ten righteous.

verses.bibleText: And the LORD appeared unto him in the plains of Mamre: and he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The chapter begins by telling the reader what Abraham himself does not yet know: “the LORD appeared unto him.” The sentence follows so closely on chapter 17 that Abraham’s name is not even repeated; the pronoun assumes we have just watched him circumcise his whole household. Both scenes look toward Isaac’s birth roughly a year away (17:21; 18:10), so only days or weeks separate them. Earlier appearances of God to Abraham were brief encounters of word and vision. This one is the most personal of all. God comes to the tent, is welcomed as a guest, and shares a meal.

The setting is precise. Mamre near Hebron was where Abraham had pitched his tent and raised an altar (13:18), and its owner had been his ally in the war against the eastern kings (14:13). Abraham is sitting “in the tent door,” the place where a host could watch the road and see anyone approaching. It is “the heat of the day,” the noon hour when travel stops and everyone looks for shade. A ninety-nine-year-old man recently circumcised had every reason to stay still. The narrative will show him doing the reverse.

The narrator uses the covenant name, YHWH, for the visitor throughout the chapter, while Abraham addresses him with the respectful title Lord. The God whom no one has seen in his full glory (John 1:18) takes a form Abraham can look upon, speak with, and serve. Old Testament appearances of the LORD in human form are best understood as the Son of God revealing the Father before his incarnation; Jesus himself said that Abraham rejoiced to see his day (John 8:56). Mamre gives an early glimpse of the Word who would one day dwell among us in flesh (John 1:14).

The opening is also built to be compared with 19:1. Abraham sits in a tent door at midday; Lot sits in the gate of Sodom at evening. The pilgrim and the city official will be tested by the same visitors, and their households will be judged by what the visit reveals.

wordNotes.term: וַיֵּרָא אֵלָיו יְהוָה (wayyera ʾelayw YHWH) — and the LORD appeared unto him
wordNotes.explanation: The verb is the passive-reflexive form of “to see,” literally “and the LORD let himself be seen” by him. It is the language of theophany used at the major turning points of Abraham’s life (12:7; 17:1) and later of Isaac and Jacob (26:2; 35:9). Seeing becomes a key thread in the chapter: Abraham lifts his eyes and sees (v. 2), and the LORD goes down to see Sodom (v. 21). The initiative is wholly God’s; Abraham does not summon the vision.

wordNotes.term: בְּאֵלֹנֵי מַמְרֵא (beʾelone mamre) — in the plains of Mamre
wordNotes.explanation: The KJV “plains” follows an older interpretation, but ʾelon refers to a large tree, probably a terebinth or oak; the Greek Old Testament renders it “oak.” Such great trees were landmarks and shelters in the hill country, and this grove was Abraham’s settled place of worship. The shade under “the tree” (v. 4) becomes the setting for the meal.

verses.bibleText: And he lift up his eyes and looked, and, lo, three men stood by him: and when he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself toward the ground,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abraham “lift up his eyes and looked, and, lo.” The phrase marks a moment of sudden perception, and it recurs in Genesis when something significant comes into view (22:13; 24:63). What he sees are “three men” standing near him. The narrator has already told us that the LORD is present, and the following chapters clarify the company: one of the three is the LORD himself, and the other two are the angels who go on to Sodom (18:22; 19:1). The suggestion that the three represent the three persons of the Godhead reads more into the scene than the text supports, since two of the visitors are explicitly called angels and act as messengers of the one LORD who stays behind with Abraham.

The men are standing by him, not calling out. In the customs of the time, a traveller who stopped near a tent was in effect knocking at the door. Abraham’s response is immediate. He “ran to meet them,” an extraordinary action for an elderly man in midday heat, and the verb “ran” will appear again when he goes to the herd (v. 7). Haste is the signature of his hospitality. He does not wait to judge whether the strangers deserve his trouble.

The bow to the ground was a customary gesture of respect toward an honoured visitor; Abraham later bows the same way before the Hittites (23:7), and Jacob before Esau (33:3). At this point the bow need not mean that Abraham recognises his God. Its importance lies in the attitude it shows: a wealthy chief makes himself the servant of passing strangers. Hebrews draws its lesson from scenes like this: some, by welcoming strangers, have entertained angels without knowing it (Hebrews 13:2). The one who comes unannounced may carry a blessing far greater than the host could imagine (Luke 24:29–31).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ אָרְצָה (wayyishtaḥu ʾartsah) — and bowed himself toward the ground
wordNotes.explanation: This verb describes full prostration, the body bent low with the face toward the earth. It can express worship of God (22:5; Exodus 34:8), but it is equally used of honour shown to human superiors or guests (23:7; 33:3; 1 Kings 2:19). The context decides which is meant. Here the gesture fits courtesy toward strangers, though the narrator’s readers already know that the honour is falling on the LORD himself.

verses.bibleText: And said, My Lord, if now I have found favour in thy sight, pass not away, I pray thee, from thy servant:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abraham’s invitation is phrased in the most deferential language of the ancient Near East. “If now I have found favour in thy sight” is the courtesy of an inferior addressing someone of higher rank (30:27; 33:10; 47:29). He calls himself “thy servant” and asks the visitor not to “pass away,” that is, not to go on by without stopping. The request turns his own convenience into a favour he begs of them, which is the art of true hospitality.

The address is singular. Abraham speaks first to one of the three, “My Lord,” and to “thy sight” and “thy servant,” before switching to the plural in verses 4–5. One visitor may have stood out as leader or spokesman, and Abraham naturally addresses him. The Hebrew vowels preserved in the received text read the title as ʾAdonay, the form used for God, rather than ʾadoni, the ordinary “my lord.” That reading may reflect the narrator’s knowledge that this guest is in fact the LORD, or it may hint that Abraham already sensed something more than human in him. Either way, the reader is meant to hear the irony: the patriarch is offering water to his Maker.

Abraham’s recognition seems to grow during the visit rather than arrive all at once. His actions in verses 4–8 are those of a host serving tired travellers, and the decisive disclosure comes when the visitor knows Sarah’s name, promises a son, and reads her unspoken laughter (vv. 9–15). God often comes to his people through ordinary channels before they understand who has come. The disciples on the road to Emmaus urged a stranger to stay, and only at the table did they recognise him (Luke 24:29–31). The plea “pass not away” stands behind every prayer that asks the Lord to abide, and it anticipates the promise of the risen Christ to enter and sup with anyone who opens the door (Revelation 3:20).

wordNotes.term: אֲדֹנָי (ʾadonay) — my Lord
wordNotes.explanation: The consonants could be read as ʾadoni (“my lord,” a polite address to a man) or ʾadonay (“my Lord,” reserved for God). The received vowel pointing chooses the divine form here, as it does in verses 27, 30–32, while Lot’s address in 19:2 is read as a plural to human guests. The narrator consistently names the visitor YHWH, so the reader understands that Abraham’s courtesy, whatever his first perception, is directed to God.

wordNotes.term: מָצָאתִי חֵן (matsaʾti ḥen) — I have found favour
wordNotes.explanation: Finding ḥen, grace or favour, in someone’s eyes means being regarded kindly by a person who has power to grant or withhold. The phrase first appears of Noah, who found grace in the eyes of the LORD (6:8). On human lips it is a respectful formula of request (32:5; 47:29). Abraham uses it as a petitioner, asking for the honour of serving.

verses.bibleText: Let a little water, I pray you, be fetched, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abraham now speaks to all three visitors in the plural. His first offer is water for their feet. Travellers on dusty roads in sandals arrived with tired and soiled feet, and providing water for washing was a basic act of welcome (19:2; 24:32; 43:24). Abraham says “let a little water … be fetched,” assigning the task to servants rather than doing it himself, yet his language keeps the offer small and easy to accept.

The second offer is rest “under the tree.” In the noonday heat, shade was itself a gift. The verb pictures the guests leaning back or reclining while the host attends to everything else. Abraham anticipates needs the travellers have not voiced: refreshment for the body, relief from the sun, and freedom from any obligation to help.

Centuries later Jesus would take water and wash his disciples’ feet, reversing the roles of host and servant to show what greatness in his kingdom looks like (John 13:4–15). Paul lists washing the saints’ feet among the marks of a faithful widow (1 Timothy 5:10). Abraham’s simple courtesy belongs to the same family of acts: care for the weary given without calculation.

The order of Abraham’s offers is worth noticing. Before food comes relief: clean feet, shade, stillness. A good host meets the most pressing needs first and lets the guest recover before anything else is asked of him. The God who later invites the weary to come to him and find rest (Matthew 11:28) is himself welcomed here with rest.

wordNotes.term: וְהִשָּׁעֲנוּ תַּחַת הָעֵץ (wehishshaʿanu taḥat haʿets) — and rest yourselves under the tree
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to lean or support oneself, here to recline at ease. It is used elsewhere of leaning on a staff or on a person for support (2 Samuel 1:6; 2 Kings 5:18). Abraham offers his guests a place to put down their weight, an image the prophets later apply to leaning on the LORD himself (Isaiah 50:10).

verses.bibleText: And I will fetch a morsel of bread, and comfort ye your hearts; after that ye shall pass on: for therefore are ye come to your servant. And they said, So do, as thou hast said.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abraham promises “a morsel of bread,” a deliberately modest phrase. Good hosts in that culture understated what they offered so that guests would not feel burdened by accepting. The meal that follows will be a feast of fine bread, choice meat, curds, and milk. The gap between the promise and the provision is part of the portrait of Abraham’s generosity.

“Comfort ye your hearts” means “strengthen yourselves” or “refresh yourselves.” Bread sustains the heart in Hebrew idiom because the heart stands for the inner person, including bodily strength and vitality (Judges 19:5; Psalm 104:15). Abraham also releases his guests from any obligation to linger: “after that ye shall pass on.” He does not seek to detain them for his own advantage. His explanation, “for therefore are ye come to your servant,” reads their arrival as an occasion providentially given him to serve.

The visitors’ reply is brief: “So do, as thou hast said.” God accepts the hospitality of a man. The LORD is not in need of food (Psalm 50:12), yet he receives what Abraham offers as an expression of friendship. Scripture calls Abraham the friend of God (2 Chronicles 20:7; James 2:23), and friendship in the ancient world was sealed at a table. The acceptance anticipates the day when Christ would eat in the homes of sinners and declare that salvation had come to them (Luke 19:5–9).

wordNotes.term: פַּת־לֶחֶם (pat-leḥem) — a morsel of bread
wordNotes.explanation: A pat is a piece broken off a flat loaf, the smallest unit of a meal. The phrase is used for minimal nourishment (Judges 19:5; 1 Samuel 28:22; Proverbs 17:1). On Abraham’s lips it is courteous understatement: he promises a scrap and serves a banquet.

wordNotes.term: וְסַעֲדוּ לִבְּכֶם (wesaʿadu libbekhem) — and comfort ye your hearts
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to support or sustain, and it is used of food that strengthens the body (Judges 19:5, 8) and of God upholding his people (Psalm 20:2; 94:18). “Heart” here is the whole inner person, including physical energy. Abraham offers what will restore their strength for the road.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham hastened into the tent unto Sarah, and said, Make ready quickly three measures of fine meal, knead it, and make cakes upon the hearth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The pace quickens. Abraham “hastened into the tent unto Sarah” and gives terse orders: “Make ready quickly.” The Hebrew piles up words of speed, and the reader feels the urgency of a host who will not keep his guests waiting. Sarah’s part in the preparation also brings her into the story, setting up the conversation that follows.

The quantity is lavish. Three seahs of flour amount to roughly twenty litres or more, far beyond what three travellers could eat. And it is “fine meal,” the best grade of flour, the kind later required for grain offerings and for the bread of the Presence in the sanctuary (Leviticus 2:1; 24:5). The cakes were round flat loaves baked quickly on hot stones or embers, suited to a meal prepared in haste.

The measure itself echoes elsewhere. Gideon prepared unleavened cakes from an ephah of flour for the Angel of the LORD (Judges 6:19), and Jesus spoke of leaven hidden in three measures of meal until the whole was leavened (Matthew 13:33). Abraham gives from his best without asking whether the gift will be fully used. Generosity of that kind reflects the character of the God who gives abundantly to those who come to him.

wordNotes.term: שְׁלֹשׁ סְאִים קֶמַח סֹלֶת (shelosh seʾim qemaḥ solet) — three measures of fine meal
wordNotes.explanation: A seah was a dry measure, probably a third of an ephah, so three seahs made about an ephah of grain. Two words for flour are combined: qemaḥ, ordinary meal, and solet, the finely ground flour reserved for honoured guests and sacred offerings (Leviticus 2:1; Ezekiel 16:13). The doubling stresses quality as well as quantity.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham ran unto the herd, and fetcht a calf tender and good, and gave it unto a young man; and he hasted to dress it.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Again Abraham “ran,” this time to the herd. He chooses the animal himself, “a calf tender and good,” and gives it to a young man who hurries to prepare it. In a pastoral economy, meat was rarely eaten; slaughtering a calf was reserved for great occasions (1 Samuel 28:24; Luke 15:23). Abraham treats unknown travellers as guests of the highest honour.

The “young man” is unnamed. He may simply be a servant, or the term may point to Ishmael, now thirteen, who is called by the same word in 21:12 and 21:17. Either way, the whole household is drawn into serving. Abraham’s personal involvement in selecting the best animal shows that the honour of the guests is his own concern, not a task he can delegate. The tender, good calf recalls the prodigal’s father, who called for the fatted calf at the return of his son: in both scenes the abundance of the feast expresses the heart of the one who gives it.

The verse moves quickly, almost breathlessly, from running to choosing to giving to preparing, so that the reader senses the whole camp stirring for these guests.

wordNotes.term: בֶּן־בָּקָר רַךְ וָטוֹב (ben-baqar rakh watov) — a calf tender and good
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “a son of the herd,” a young animal from the cattle. Rakh means soft or tender and tov here describes quality, the choicest of the herd. Young unblemished animals from the herd were later prescribed for offerings (Leviticus 1:5; 9:2), and the fatted calf became a symbol of celebration (Luke 15:23).

verses.bibleText: And he took butter, and milk, and the calf which he had dressed, and set it before them; and he stood by them under the tree, and they did eat.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abraham sets before his guests “butter, and milk, and the calf.” The “butter” was most likely curds or thickened soured milk, a refreshing food in a hot climate and a prized part of a pastoral meal (Judges 5:25; Isaiah 7:15). Together with the fresh bread and tender meat, it made a full banquet, the best a prosperous pastoral household could offer.

Abraham “stood by them under the tree” while they ate. The host does not sit down with his guests; he waits on them like a servant, ready to supply what they need. The posture fits the honour he has shown from the start, and it hints that he is beginning to perceive who his guests are.

The statement “they did eat” is remarkable. The LORD and the angels actually ate the food Abraham prepared. This was no dream or vision but a real visit in tangible form, and their eating confirmed it. The risen Christ would do the same, eating broiled fish before his disciples to prove that he was no phantom (Luke 24:41–43). Elsewhere in the Old Testament heavenly visitors decline food or turn it into an offering (Judges 6:21; 13:16). Here God receives Abraham’s hospitality as a friend at table, and that shared meal becomes the setting for the promise.

The scene foreshadows a larger table. Jesus spoke of many coming from east and west to sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom (Matthew 8:11), and of the Lord who will gird himself and serve his faithful servants at his return (Luke 12:37). At Mamre the human host serves God; in the kingdom the divine Host will serve his people.

wordNotes.term: חֶמְאָה (ḥemʾah) — butter
wordNotes.explanation: The word denotes curdled or thickened milk, closer to yogurt or soft curds than to churned butter. It was offered to guests as a refreshing delicacy (Judges 5:25) and appears among the foods of abundance in a land flowing with milk (Deuteronomy 32:14; Isaiah 7:22).

wordNotes.term: וְהוּא־עֹמֵד עֲלֵיהֶם (wehuʾ-ʿomed ʿalehem) — and he stood by them
wordNotes.explanation: To stand over or beside those who are seated is the posture of a servant in attendance (1 Kings 10:8; Zechariah 4:14). The participle depicts ongoing readiness. The same verb will return when Abraham stands before the LORD to intercede (v. 22).

verses.bibleText: And they said unto him, Where is Sarah thy wife? And he said, Behold, in the tent.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
When the meal is over, the guests ask a question no ordinary traveller would ask: “Where is Sarah thy wife?” Custom kept women apart from male visitors, and strangers would not normally know a wife’s name, still less inquire after her. Sarah’s name had been given by God only recently (17:15). That the visitors use it signals that they know more than they have been told, and it shifts the conversation from hospitality to revelation.

The question is not a request for information. Like “Where art thou?” to Adam (3:9) and “Where is Abel thy brother?” to Cain (4:9), it is God’s way of opening a matter he already knows. Here the purpose is gracious. The visit concerns Sarah, and the question draws her attention, as she listens from inside the tent, to what is about to be said about her.

Abraham answers simply: “Behold, in the tent.” Sarah is near enough to hear and far enough to stay unseen. The promise of chapter 17 had been spoken to Abraham alone; now it will be repeated where Sarah can receive it for herself.

wordNotes.term: אַיֵּה (ʾayyeh) — where
wordNotes.explanation: This interrogative is used when God asks questions to which he knows the answer, inviting a response rather than gaining information (3:9 uses a related form; 4:9). The prophets use it to challenge Israel about the presence of God among them (Jeremiah 2:6, 8). Here it turns the guests’ attention, and the reader’s, toward Sarah.

verses.bibleText: And he said, I will certainly return unto thee according to the time of life; and, lo, Sarah thy wife shall have a son. And Sarah heard it in the tent door, which was behind him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The speaker changes from “they” to “he.” One guest now speaks, and what he says only the LORD could promise: “I will certainly return unto thee according to the time of life; and, lo, Sarah thy wife shall have a son.” A king might promise land or wealth, but no human visitor could guarantee that a barren woman of eighty-nine would bear a child, still less fix the time. The promise repeats the substance of 17:19 and 17:21, now with Sarah within earshot.

“According to the time of life” is an unusual expression. It probably means “when the time comes round again,” that is, at this season next year, which is how Paul cites the promise in Romans 9:9 and how the Greek Old Testament understood it. Some take it to mean the time of a pregnancy’s completion. Either way the birth is set within a defined horizon. Promises that had stretched over twenty-five years since Haran (12:4) are now compressed into months.

“I will certainly return” uses the emphatic doubled verb. The LORD’s return in 21:1, when he “visited Sarah as he had said,” fulfils this word. His coming back is a pledge of personal intervention: Isaac’s conception will be the LORD’s own act.

The narrator adds that Sarah “heard it in the tent door, which was behind him.” The speaker has his back to the tent. He cannot see her, yet in verse 13 he will report her inward thought exactly. That detail prepares the reader to recognise the visitor’s divine knowledge. Paul reads this promise as the word that created the line of promise: the children of Abraham are counted by God’s pledge, not by natural descent alone (Romans 9:7–9). Isaac is born because God spoke.

wordNotes.term: כָּעֵת חַיָּה (kaʿet ḥayyah) — according to the time of life
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “as the time living,” the phrase is found only here, in verse 14, and in 2 Kings 4:16–17, where Elisha promises the Shunammite a son. In both places it marks the coming round of the same season a year later. The Greek Old Testament renders it “at this time, at the season,” and Paul quotes it in that sense.

wordNotes.term: שׁוֹב אָשׁוּב (shov ʾashuv) — I will certainly return
wordNotes.explanation: The infinitive placed before the finite verb intensifies the statement: “returning, I will return.” Hebrew uses the construction to express certainty or emphasis (2:17; 3:4 use it with “die”). The return is fulfilled when the LORD “visited” Sarah (21:1).

verses.bibleText: Now Abraham and Sarah were old and well stricken in age; and it ceased to be with Sarah after the manner of women.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The narrator pauses the dialogue to explain why the promise sounds impossible. “Abraham and Sarah were old and well stricken in age.” Abraham is ninety-nine and Sarah eighty-nine (17:17). The phrase “well stricken in age” means literally “gone far into the days,” a way of describing people who have reached the far end of life.

The second clause is more specific: “it ceased to be with Sarah after the manner of women.” Her monthly cycle had stopped. Barrenness had marked her all her life (11:30), and now her body was beyond childbearing by any natural measure. Paul uses this very fact to describe the quality of Abraham’s faith: he considered his own body “now dead” and “the deadness of Sarah’s womb,” and still did not stagger at the promise (Romans 4:19–20). Hebrews says Sarah herself received strength to conceive “when she was past age” (Hebrews 11:11).

Scripture repeatedly lets human possibility run out before God acts, so that the result can only be credited to him. Isaac’s birth is a sign of resurrection power, life given where there was no life. The same power raised Jesus from the dead (Romans 4:24).

Luke tells the story of Zechariah and Elizabeth in language that deliberately recalls this verse: they too were righteous, childless, and “well stricken in years” (Luke 1:7). In both accounts the promised child arrives only when every human expectation has been exhausted, and the birth announces a new stage in God’s saving purpose.

wordNotes.term: בָּאִים בַּיָּמִים (baʾim bayyamim) — well stricken in age
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “coming into the days,” an idiom for advanced age used of Abraham again in 24:1, of Joshua (Joshua 13:1), and of David (1 Kings 1:1). Luke uses the equivalent Greek phrase of Zechariah and Elizabeth before John’s birth (Luke 1:7), deliberately echoing this scene.

wordNotes.term: אֹרַח כַּנָּשִׁים (ʾoraḥ kannashim) — after the manner of women
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the way like women,” a delicate expression for menstruation, used also by Rachel in 31:35. Its cessation meant that conception had become naturally impossible for Sarah.

verses.bibleText: Therefore Sarah laughed within herself, saying, After I am waxed old shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Therefore Sarah laughed within herself.” Her laughter is silent, an inward reaction she assumes no one can detect. Abraham had laughed at the same promise in 17:17, falling on his face. Both parents laugh, and the son will be named Isaac, “he laughs” (17:19; 21:3), so that their incredulity is turned into the very name of the gift.

Sarah’s thought is honest about her condition: “After I am waxed old shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?” “Waxed old” uses a verb for something worn out, like a garment. The word translated “pleasure” is rare and has been understood as delight, fruitfulness, or the renewal of youthful vigour; in context it refers to the joys of conjugal love and childbearing that she had long ago given up. Her laugh is likely a mixture of disbelief and weary sadness. For decades the promise had been repeated and nothing had changed, and hope had become painful.

She calls Abraham “my lord,” even in her private thought. Peter seizes on this detail to commend her respect for her husband as an example for Christian wives (1 Peter 3:6). The narrative holds together her failing and her virtue without excusing one or erasing the other.

Sarah’s response is very human. She measures the promise by what her body can do and finds it laughable. Faith begins elsewhere: with the One who promises. The next verses do not condemn her to rejection. They move her from looking at her own deadness to looking at the LORD’s power.

wordNotes.term: וַתִּצְחַק (wattitsḥaq) — and she laughed
wordNotes.explanation: The verb tsaḥaq, “to laugh,” forms the basis of the name Yitsḥaq, Isaac. It runs through the story: Abraham laughs (17:17), Sarah laughs in doubt here, she laughs in joy at the birth (21:6), and Ishmael’s mocking is described with a related form (21:9). The same root can carry unbelief, joy, or derision, and the context sets its colour.

wordNotes.term: עֶדְנָה (ʿednah) — pleasure
wordNotes.explanation: This exact form occurs only here. It is related to the word for delight or luxury, which also lies behind the name Eden (2:8). Ancient translators variously took it as delight, renewed youth, or conception. Sarah means the vitality and joy of bearing a child, long lost to her.

verses.bibleText: And the LORD said unto Abraham, Wherefore did Sarah laugh, saying, Shall I of a surety bear a child, which am old?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Now the narrator says plainly what the reader has known from verse 1: “the LORD said unto Abraham.” The visitor reveals himself by knowing what no guest could know. Sarah laughed inwardly, behind him and out of sight, yet he repeats her thought almost word for word. Only God searches the heart and understands unspoken thoughts (1 Samuel 16:7; Psalm 139:1–4; Hebrews 4:13).

The LORD addresses his question to Abraham rather than Sarah: “Wherefore did Sarah laugh?” He respects the custom of the household and lets Abraham, who already believes the promise (Romans 4:20), stand between. Yet Sarah hears every word. The question is a rebuke, but it is a rebuke meant to heal. Its purpose is to show her that the one making the promise knows her completely and has come specifically for her.

The LORD’s paraphrase of her thought slightly reshapes it. Sarah had mentioned both her age and Abraham’s; the LORD repeats only the part about herself, “which am old,” and leaves out her remark about her husband. The detail is small, but it shows tact even in correction, sparing Abraham the sting of her comment. Jesus likewise read the thoughts of those around him (Mark 2:8; John 2:25), and his knowledge of the heart was both a warning and a comfort.

wordNotes.term: הַאַף אֻמְנָם (haʾaf ʾumnam) — shall I of a surety
wordNotes.explanation: The two particles combine to express incredulous questioning: “Shall I really and truly …?” Uttered in the LORD’s report of Sarah’s thought, they capture her disbelief. The second word is related to the verb for being firm or trustworthy (15:6), so that the question of whether something is “truly” so sits close to the issue of faith.

verses.bibleText: Is any thing too hard for the LORD? At the time appointed I will return unto thee, according to the time of life, and Sarah shall have a son.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Is any thing too hard for the LORD?” This question stands at the centre of the chapter and is one of the great sentences of Scripture. It answers Sarah’s laughter not with an argument about her body but with a statement about God. The issue is not whether a woman of eighty-nine can conceive; it is whether there exists anything beyond the reach of the LORD who made heaven and earth.

The verb translated “too hard” means to be extraordinary, wonderful, beyond what is ordinarily possible. It is the language of miracle. The same root describes the wonders God did in Egypt (Exodus 3:20), the counsel of the Child who would be called “Wonderful” (Isaiah 9:6), and Jeremiah’s confession, “there is nothing too hard for thee” (Jeremiah 32:17), to which the LORD answered with this very question (Jeremiah 32:27). What lies outside human power is not outside his. Indeed, God often lets circumstances reach the point of impossibility so that the gift can be recognised as his alone.

The promise is then repeated with a new detail: “At the time appointed.” The birth is set on God’s calendar. The word for appointed time is used for fixed seasons and sacred occasions (1:14; Leviticus 23:2). Isaac will come neither early nor late, but at the moment God has determined, just as Paul says that Christ was sent “when the fulness of the time was come” (Galatians 4:4).

The angel Gabriel echoed this verse when he told Mary that her elderly cousin Elizabeth had conceived and added, “For with God nothing shall be impossible” (Luke 1:36–37). Jesus said the same about the salvation of those who seem beyond hope (Mark 10:27). The God who gave Isaac to Sarah gave his Son through a virgin and raised him from the grave. The question at Mamre still meets every situation where human strength has failed: faith rests on what God can do, not on what we can see.

wordNotes.term: הֲיִפָּלֵא מֵיְהוָה דָּבָר (hayippaleʾ meYHWH davar) — is any thing too hard for the LORD
wordNotes.explanation: The verb palaʾ in this form means to be extraordinary, surpassing, or too wonderful. It describes matters beyond human ability to perform or understand (Deuteronomy 17:8; Psalm 139:6) and, above all, God’s saving wonders (Exodus 3:20; Psalm 136:4). Davar can mean both “word” and “thing,” so the question can be heard as “Is any word too wonderful for the LORD to fulfil?” The Greek Old Testament uses the same idea that Luke 1:37 echoes in the announcement to Mary.

wordNotes.term: לַמּוֹעֵד (lammoʿed) — at the time appointed
wordNotes.explanation: Moʿed is a fixed time or meeting, used for the seasons governed by the heavenly lights (1:14), the feasts of Israel (Leviticus 23:2), and the set time of prophetic fulfilment (Habakkuk 2:3). It repeats the language of 17:21 and is fulfilled in 21:2, where Sarah bears Isaac “at the set time.”

verses.bibleText: Then Sarah denied, saying, I laughed not; for she was afraid. And he said, Nay; but thou didst laugh.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Sarah now speaks directly, perhaps stepping from behind the tent curtain: “I laughed not.” The narrator explains why: “for she was afraid.” She had not expected to be heard, and the sudden exposure of her private thought by a stranger who now speaks as the LORD filled her with alarm. Fear led her to deny what she had done. Scripture does not hide the faults of its heroes and heroines; Abraham had lied about Sarah in Egypt (12:13), and here Sarah lies about herself.

The LORD’s reply is short and firm: “Nay; but thou didst laugh.” He does not argue or explain. As in Eden, when he questioned Adam and Eve with direct words (3:11–13), God refuses to let the falsehood stand. Yet the rebuke carries hope. The One who knew her laughter also knew her future. His correction was proof that he saw her completely, and the same knowledge that exposed her doubt guaranteed his promise to her.

The narrative records no defence and no further words from Sarah. Her silence suggests conviction. In time her laughter of unbelief would become laughter of joy: “God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me” (21:6). Hebrews counts her among the heroes of faith, who judged him faithful who had promised (Hebrews 11:11). God did not wait for her faith to be perfect before keeping his word; his grace worked on her doubt and brought her to trust. Those who struggle to believe may bring their fears into the open before God, who forgives the sins we confess (1 John 1:9).

wordNotes.term: וַתְּכַחֵשׁ (wattekhaḥesh) — then she denied
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to deceive, deny, or act falsely, often in contexts of disowning the truth (Leviticus 6:2; Joshua 24:27; Proverbs 30:9). It is used of breaking faith with God or a neighbour. Sarah’s denial is a small but real falsehood, prompted by fear.

wordNotes.term: כִּי יָרֵאָה (ki yareʾah) — for she was afraid
wordNotes.explanation: Fear is the first emotion named after the fall: “I was afraid … and I hid myself” (3:10). Sarah’s fear springs from being uncovered before God. The remedy is the divine word heard elsewhere in Genesis, “Fear not” (15:1; 21:17).

verses.bibleText: And the men rose up from thence, and looked toward Sodom: and Abraham went with them to bring them on the way.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The visit turns. “The men rose up from thence, and looked toward Sodom.” For the first time the guests’ destination is named, and with it the mood of the chapter darkens. The verb for looking implies gazing down from a height. From the hills near Hebron one could see across the wilderness toward the valley of the Dead Sea, where the cities of the plain lay. The same verb is used later when the LORD “looked” upon the Egyptian army before overthrowing it (Exodus 14:24), and it often carries a hint of judgment.

The visitors who brought life to Abraham’s tent now face the city that will receive their judgment. The verse is a hinge: behind lies a promise of birth, ahead a sentence of destruction. Both come from the same LORD, who “killeth, and maketh alive” (1 Samuel 2:6).

Abraham “went with them to bring them on the way.” Escorting departing guests some distance was a customary mark of honour and friendship, practised into New Testament times (Acts 20:38; 3 John 1:6). Abraham’s courtesy keeps him in the company of the LORD, and his walk with his guests becomes the occasion for the most remarkable conversation of his life. Those who walk with God find themselves taken into his counsel.

wordNotes.term: וַיַּשְׁקִפוּ (wayyashqifu) — and looked toward
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to look down, as from a window or a height (26:8; 2 Samuel 6:16). When God is the subject, it often describes looking down from heaven, sometimes in blessing (Deuteronomy 26:15) and sometimes in judgment (Exodus 14:24). Abraham himself will look down on the smoking plain the next morning (19:28).

wordNotes.term: לְשַׁלְּחָם (leshallḥam) — to bring them on the way
wordNotes.explanation: The intensive form of the verb “to send” here means to escort or see someone off courteously (31:27; 1 Kings 8:66). Elsewhere the same form can mean to dismiss or send away, but here it is an act of hospitality.

verses.bibleText: And the LORD said, Shall I hide from Abraham that thing which I do;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The narrator lets the reader overhear the LORD’s thought: “Shall I hide from Abraham that thing which I do?” The question is a deliberation spoken within the divine council, perhaps to the two angels who accompany him. It reveals the reason for the conversation that follows. God has decided to take Abraham into his confidence about Sodom before he acts.

The reason lies in relationship. Abraham is the friend of God (2 Chronicles 20:7; Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23), and friendship involves disclosure. Jesus put it this way to his disciples: servants do not know what their master is doing, but friends are told what the Father has made known (John 15:15). Amos stated the principle for the prophets: “Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets” (Amos 3:7). In Genesis 20:7 God himself calls Abraham a prophet.

The disclosure especially concerns judgment. God does not act in hidden arbitrariness. He warned Noah before the flood (6:13), he warns Abraham before Sodom, and he gives his people prophetic warning before the final judgments of earth (Revelation 14:6–7). The God who could act without explanation chooses to make his ways known, so that those who love him may understand his justice and plead for mercy while there is still time.

The verse also shows that the coming judgment is already settled in principle; the investigation that follows (v. 21) does not mean God is uncertain. It means his justice will be displayed openly, with his friend as witness.

The setting adds weight to the decision. God is walking with Abraham along the road, the patriarch escorting his guest as a friend escorts a friend. Revelation comes in the course of fellowship. Abraham did not seek out the secret of Sodom; it was offered to him because he was already walking in step with the LORD, as Enoch and Noah had walked with God before him (5:24; 6:9).

wordNotes.term: הַמְכַסֶּה אֲנִי (hamekhasseh ʾani) — shall I hide
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to cover or conceal. Its participle with the pronoun gives the question force: “Am I one who conceals …?” God’s readiness to reveal contrasts with sinners who try to cover their sin (Proverbs 28:13) and with Sarah, who had just tried to hide her laughter. The secret of the LORD is with those who fear him (Psalm 25:14).

verses.bibleText: Seeing that Abraham shall surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The first reason for including Abraham is his calling. “Abraham shall surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him.” The LORD recalls the original promise of 12:2–3 and makes it the ground for sharing his plans. Abraham is not only a private believer; he is the head of a people through whom God intends to bless the world.

That calling links Abraham directly to Sodom. Sodom is one of the nations of the earth. If blessing is to flow to the nations through Abraham, he must understand why one city is about to be removed from the opportunity of that blessing. The land of Canaan had also been promised to his descendants (13:14–17), and a judgment falling within that land concerned him as heir. His nephew Lot lived in the city. For all these reasons it was fitting that the friend of God should know what was coming and be given room to respond.

The promise that “all the nations” would be blessed in Abraham is fulfilled in Christ, his seed (Galatians 3:8, 16). The gospel preached beforehand to Abraham has a global horizon. Even as judgment approaches Sodom, God speaks of blessing for the whole world. Peter announced that same blessing to Jerusalem, calling his hearers to turn from their iniquities (Acts 3:25–26).

wordNotes.term: וְנִבְרְכוּ בוֹ (wenivrekhu vo) — shall be blessed in him
wordNotes.explanation: The passive-reflexive form of “bless” here is the same as in 12:3 and 28:14. It promises that the nations will find blessing through their relationship to Abraham. Paul reads it as the gospel announced in advance, fulfilled when Gentiles are justified by faith in Abraham’s seed, Christ (Galatians 3:8).

verses.bibleText: For I know him, that he will command his children and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the LORD, to do justice and judgment; that the LORD may bring upon Abraham that which he hath spoken of him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The second reason is Abraham’s responsibility. “For I know him, that he will command his children and his household after him.” The verb “know” here expresses more than awareness. It describes a personal, elective relationship: God has chosen Abraham and drawn him into intimacy, as he “knew” Jeremiah before his birth (Jeremiah 1:5) and “knew” Israel above all the families of the earth (Amos 3:2). Many modern versions render it “I have chosen him.”

The purpose of that choice is stated at once. Abraham is to command his children and household so that “they shall keep the way of the LORD, to do justice and judgment.” Election is not an end in itself. God chose Abraham to form a people who would live according to his character. “The way of the LORD” is the whole pattern of life that follows his direction; “justice and judgment,” literally righteousness and justice, describe a life that treats others rightly and upholds what is right in community (Psalm 33:5; Proverbs 21:3). The words stand in pointed contrast to the outcry rising from Sodom in the next verse.

This instruction begins in the home. Abraham is pictured as priest, prophet, and teacher to his household, which included hundreds of servants (14:14). The pattern is later written into Israel’s law: parents are to teach God’s words diligently to their children, at home and on the road (Deuteronomy 6:6–7). The faith of the next generation is not left to chance. It is shaped by clear instruction and, above all, by consistent example. Firmness and love go together; what a father commands is credible only when he walks in it himself.

The final clause links obedience to promise: “that the LORD may bring upon Abraham that which he hath spoken of him.” God’s promises are unconditional in their source, resting on his grace alone, yet he fulfils them through the faithful obedience of those he has called. Genesis later says that Abraham “obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws” (26:5), long before Sinai. Obedience did not earn Abraham’s election; it was the fruit God intended that election to bear (Ephesians 2:8–10).

wordNotes.term: יְדַעְתִּיו (yedaʿtiw) — I know him
wordNotes.explanation: The verb yadaʿ often includes personal commitment and choice, especially when God is the subject (Exodus 33:12, 17; Jeremiah 1:5; Amos 3:2). It describes a relationship God initiates rather than mere awareness of facts. In this verse it introduces a purpose: God knows Abraham in order that Abraham will teach his household.

wordNotes.term: צְדָקָה וּמִשְׁפָּט (tsedaqah umishpat) — justice and judgment
wordNotes.explanation: The pair, usually translated “righteousness and justice,” appears often in the prophets and Psalms. Tsedaqah is right conduct that conforms to God’s standard and maintains right relationships; mishpat is just decision and action, especially in defending the wronged. God himself loves and practises both (Psalm 33:5; Jeremiah 9:24), and he looks for them in his people (Isaiah 5:7; Amos 5:24).

verses.bibleText: And the LORD said, Because the cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and because their sin is very grievous;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The LORD now speaks openly about Sodom. “Because the cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and because their sin is very grievous.” The word “cry” is the outcry of the wronged, a scream for help raised by those who suffer violence or oppression (Exodus 3:7, 9; Isaiah 5:7). Like Abel’s blood crying from the ground (4:10), the suffering caused in these cities has reached heaven. God hears the cry of victims who have no human advocate.

In Hebrew the word for “cry” (zeʿaqah) echoes the word “righteousness” (tsedaqah) in the previous verse. Isaiah would later use the same wordplay: God looked for righteousness, but behold a cry (Isaiah 5:7). Abraham’s household is to be marked by righteousness; Sodom is marked by an outcry. The two ways stand side by side.

The sin is “very grievous,” literally “very heavy.” Genesis had already described the men of Sodom as “wicked and sinners before the LORD exceedingly” (13:13). Chapter 19 will reveal one dimension of that wickedness: an entire city ready to commit violent sexual assault against strangers (19:4–9), which Jude describes as going after strange flesh (Jude 1:7). Ezekiel adds that Sodom was proud, overfed, and at ease, and did not help the poor and needy (Ezekiel 16:49–50). Sexual perversion, violence, arrogance, and indifference to the vulnerable belong together in the biblical portrait.

The LORD’s patience had been long. Sodom had been rescued once through Abraham (14:16), its king had heard Abraham confess the Most High God (14:22), and the city had Lot living within it, whose righteous soul was vexed by their deeds (2 Peter 2:7–8). Yet the city filled up its measure of sin. Jesus warned that the days before his return would resemble the days of Lot, with life going on as normal until the sudden moment of judgment (Luke 17:28–30).

wordNotes.term: זַעֲקַת (zaʿaqat) — the cry of
wordNotes.explanation: Zeʿaqah and its variant tseʿaqah (used in v. 21 and 19:13) denote a loud outcry for help, typically from those in distress or under oppression (Exodus 2:23; 3:9; Job 34:28). It can mean the cry raised against a city because of its crimes. The phrase implies victims whose suffering has reached God’s ears.

wordNotes.term: כָּבְדָה (kavedah) — very grievous
wordNotes.explanation: The verb kaved means to be heavy. Sin is pictured as a weight, piling up until it becomes intolerable (Psalm 38:4; Isaiah 1:4). The same root, with a different sense, can describe glory, the weight of honour (Exodus 16:7).

verses.bibleText: I will go down now, and see whether they have done altogether according to the cry of it, which is come unto me; and if not, I will know.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“I will go down now, and see whether they have done altogether according to the cry of it, which is come unto me; and if not, I will know.” The language is deliberately human. As at Babel, where the LORD “came down to see the city and the tower” (11:5), God is portrayed as a judge who investigates before he pronounces sentence. The point is not that God lacks information; he knows the end from the beginning and searches every heart (Psalm 139:1–3). The point is that his judgment is never based on rumour, never hasty, and never arbitrary.

The investigation also serves those who watch. By going down to see, God makes the grounds of his judgment open and verifiable. Abraham, the angels, and the readers of Genesis will all see that the cry against Sodom was true. In the next chapter, the two angels experience the city’s violence for themselves (19:4–11), and two witnesses confirm the case, in keeping with the later principle that judgment rests on the testimony of two or three (Deuteronomy 19:15).

The phrase “and if not, I will know” leaves a door open. The outcome is not announced in advance as a foregone conclusion. God is willing to be shown that the city is not as wicked as the cry suggests, and that opening invites Abraham’s intercession. Mercy is always seeking room within justice.

Scripture presents this pattern throughout: investigation, verdict, execution. The LORD examined Adam and Eve (3:9–13) and questioned Cain (4:9–10) before passing sentence. Daniel saw the books opened in a heavenly court before the kingdom was given to the saints (Daniel 7:9–10). The God of Scripture judges openly, so that his righteousness is vindicated before the whole universe and every created being can say that his ways are just and true (Revelation 15:3).

wordNotes.term: אֵרְדָה־נָּא וְאֶרְאֶה (ʾeredah-nnaʾ weʾerʾeh) — I will go down now, and see
wordNotes.explanation: The pairing of “go down” and “see” recalls 11:5, 7, where the LORD comes down to Babel. It also anticipates Exodus 3:8, where he comes down to deliver Israel after hearing their cry. God’s descent may bring judgment or salvation depending on what he finds. The particle naʾ adds a note of resolve.

wordNotes.term: כָּלָה (kalah) — altogether
wordNotes.explanation: The word means complete or full end. It may be read as “whether they have done completely according to the cry,” or as anticipating “complete destruction” if they have. The same noun describes full destruction in judgment elsewhere (Isaiah 10:23; Jeremiah 30:11). Its position suggests that the extent of Sodom’s guilt will determine the extent of its end.

verses.bibleText: And the men turned their faces from thence, and went toward Sodom: but Abraham stood yet before the LORD.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“The men turned their faces from thence, and went toward Sodom.” The two angels go down to the city, where they arrive that evening (19:1). The LORD remains behind. “But Abraham stood yet before the LORD.” The scene narrows to two figures on the hillside: the patriarch and his God.

To “stand before” someone is the posture of a servant ready to hear and respond (1 Kings 17:1; Jeremiah 15:1). Abraham, who had stood by his guests while they ate (v. 8), now stands before the LORD in a different kind of service. He has heard what God intends, and he does not walk away. He lingers in God’s presence because he has something to say.

An ancient scribal tradition records that the original wording may have been “the LORD stood yet before Abraham,” and that copyists reversed the order out of reverence, since standing before someone could suggest inferiority. If so, the original phrasing would picture God waiting for Abraham to speak, inviting the intercession that follows. Whichever reading is adopted, the effect is similar. God has opened the conversation by disclosing his plan and leaving room with the words “if not, I will know” (v. 21). Abraham steps into that opening.

Scripture calls such people intercessors: those who “stand in the gap” before God for the land (Ezekiel 22:30). Moses stood in the breach for Israel (Psalm 106:23), and Samuel would not sin by ceasing to pray for the people (1 Samuel 12:23). Abraham is the first in that line.

wordNotes.term: עֹמֵד לִפְנֵי יְהוָה (ʿomed lifne YHWH) — stood before the LORD
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase describes attendance in the presence of a superior, often in priestly or prophetic service (Deuteronomy 10:8; 1 Kings 17:1; 18:15). It is also used of intercessors who stand before God on behalf of others (Jeremiah 15:1; 18:20). The participle shows Abraham remaining in that posture.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham drew near, and said, Wilt thou also destroy the righteous with the wicked?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Abraham drew near.” The verb describes approaching someone to speak with purpose, as Judah came near to Joseph to plead for Benjamin (44:18). In worship contexts it describes coming near to God at the altar (Exodus 28:43). Abraham’s approach combines boldness with reverence. He knows the One before whom he stands, and still he comes close.

His first words are a question that goes to the heart of divine justice: “Wilt thou also destroy the righteous with the wicked?” The verb “destroy” pictures sweeping away, removing everything together. Abraham’s concern is whether the coming judgment will make any distinction between those who do right and those who do evil. In the ancient world, destruction of a city fell on all its inhabitants. Abraham asks whether the LORD’s judgment will be like that.

Abraham’s compassion reaches beyond his own family. Lot is surely in his mind, yet he never names him. His plea is broader, embracing whatever righteous people may live in the city, and, as the dialogue will show, the city as a whole. Abraham had fought for Sodom once (14:14–16) and knew its people. He does not rejoice at their coming ruin. He seeks their preservation.

This is the first extended prayer of intercession in the Bible. It sets a pattern for all who pray for others. It is grounded in what God has revealed, it appeals to his character, and it is offered by one who stands near to him. The New Testament urges the same boldness: “Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16), and “Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you” (James 4:8). The prayer of a righteous man, James says, avails much (James 5:16).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּגַּשׁ (wayyiggash) — and drew near
wordNotes.explanation: Nagash means to approach, often with a request or for a serious encounter (27:21; 44:18). It is used of priests approaching God’s altar (Exodus 28:43) and of the people approaching God in worship or petition (Jeremiah 30:21). The word marks Abraham’s prayer as a deliberate coming into God’s presence.

wordNotes.term: הַאַף תִּסְפֶּה (haʾaf tispeh) — wilt thou also destroy
wordNotes.explanation: The verb safah means to sweep away or snatch away completely. It appears again in verse 24 and in 19:15, 17, where Lot is warned lest he be “consumed” with the city. Abraham fears an indiscriminate end in which the righteous are swept away with the guilty.

verses.bibleText: Peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city: wilt thou also destroy and not spare the place for the fifty righteous that are therein?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city.” Abraham begins with a hypothesis. Fifty is a substantial number, perhaps a sizeable portion of a small town (Amos 5:3 pictures a town that can send a hundred men to war). He asks not merely that the fifty be spared, but that the whole city be spared for their sake: “wilt thou also destroy and not spare the place for the fifty righteous that are therein?”

The request reverses ordinary thinking. Human justice often lets the guilty majority bring ruin on the innocent minority. Abraham asks whether the presence of the righteous might instead bring preservation to the guilty. The righteous become the reason for mercy. This idea of a remnant whose presence preserves a community runs through Scripture (Isaiah 1:9; 6:13) and comes to its fullest expression in the one Righteous Servant through whom many are spared (Isaiah 53:11).

The word “spare” literally means to lift up or bear. It can mean to forgive, to lift away guilt, or to show favour. Abraham is asking God to bear with the city, to hold back judgment for the sake of the righteous within it.

wordNotes.term: אוּלַי (ʾulay) — peradventure
wordNotes.explanation: The particle means “perhaps” or “suppose,” introducing a possibility not yet known. Abraham uses it six times in this dialogue (vv. 24, 28–32). It expresses humble uncertainty about what the LORD will find, combined with hope (Exodus 32:30; Amos 5:15).

wordNotes.term: תִשָּׂא (tissaʾ) — spare
wordNotes.explanation: The verb nasaʾ means to lift, carry, or bear. With sin as its object it means to forgive, to bear guilt away (Exodus 34:7; Psalm 32:1; Micah 7:18). Here Abraham asks the LORD to “bear” the place, holding back judgment so that the city may continue.

verses.bibleText: That be far from thee to do after this manner, to slay the righteous with the wicked: and that the righteous should be as the wicked, that be far from thee: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abraham presses his case with intense language. “That be far from thee to do after this manner, to slay the righteous with the wicked.” He repeats the expression “that be far from thee” twice, framing the verse. The phrase is a strong exclamation of horror at something unthinkable, as though Abraham were saying, “It would be profane for you to do such a thing!” He is not threatening God. He is appealing to what he knows God to be.

He states the principle he is defending: “that the righteous should be as the wicked.” If God treated both alike, his judgment would erase the moral distinction that gives life meaning. The Psalms rest on the conviction that the LORD knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the ungodly shall perish (Psalm 1:6), and Malachi promises that the day will come when people will discern between the righteous and the wicked (Malachi 3:18).

Then comes the climactic question: “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?” Here Abraham reaches the foundation of his prayer. He addresses the LORD as the supreme Judge, not a local god of one people or territory, but the one who governs “all the earth.” Every nation, including Sodom, is under his authority. And precisely because he is Judge of all, his judgments must be just. The question is not a doubt but a declaration of faith in the form of a question. Abraham is confident of the answer.

This is the first time Scripture calls God “Judge,” and the title shapes the rest of the Bible’s story. The Judge of all the earth will one day judge the world in righteousness by the Man whom he has ordained, Jesus Christ (Acts 17:31). Paul answers objections against divine justice by asking, “Is God unrighteous who taketh vengeance? God forbid: for then how shall God judge the world?” (Romans 3:5–6). The final judgment is not a reckless burning of everything; it is a careful separation in which every case is weighed. Peter cites Sodom as an example of God’s judgment, the cities turned to ashes, and in the same breath affirms that the Lord knows how to deliver the godly (2 Peter 2:6–9). The fire that fell on Sodom completed its work and left ruins. It did not burn without end. It brought the wicked to an end, and so will the final judgment (Malachi 4:1).

The answer to Abraham’s question is finally given at the cross, where the Judge of all the earth proved himself both just and the justifier of the one who believes in Jesus (Romans 3:26).

wordNotes.term: חָלִלָה לְּךָ (ḥalilah lekha) — that be far from thee
wordNotes.explanation: The expression comes from a root meaning to profane or treat as common. It is an exclamation rejecting something as unthinkable or sacrilegious (44:7, 17; 1 Samuel 24:6; Job 34:10). Abraham uses it to say that such a deed would be contrary to God’s holy character. The Greek Old Testament renders it with a phrase similar to Paul’s “God forbid.”

wordNotes.term: הֲשֹׁפֵט כָּל־הָאָרֶץ לֹא יַעֲשֶׂה מִשְׁפָּט (hashofet kol-haʾarets loʾ yaʿaseh mishpat) — shall not the Judge of all the earth do right
wordNotes.explanation: Shofet is the one who judges, rules, and delivers justice. Mishpat is the just decision he renders. The wordplay ties the person to the act: the Judge must do judgment. The phrase anticipates the Psalms that celebrate the LORD who comes to judge the earth with righteousness and equity (Psalm 96:13; 98:9).

verses.bibleText: And the LORD said, If I find in Sodom fifty righteous within the city, then I will spare all the place for their sakes.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The LORD answers without hesitation: “If I find in Sodom fifty righteous within the city, then I will spare all the place for their sakes.” He accepts Abraham’s proposal in full. God agrees that the presence of fifty righteous would be reason enough to spare the whole city.

The answer goes beyond justice. Justice requires that the righteous not be destroyed with the wicked; it does not require that the wicked be spared because of the righteous. To spare the guilty for the sake of the innocent is an act of mercy. God shows himself willing to extend grace to an entire city that did not deserve it, provided a righteous core existed within it. A righteous community within the city would also have provided a continuing witness, offering hope that others might yet turn.

This principle reveals God’s heart. He has no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live (Ezekiel 33:11). He waited in the days of Noah while the ark was being prepared (1 Peter 3:20), and he is longsuffering toward us, not willing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9). In Jeremiah’s day he promised to pardon Jerusalem if even one man could be found who did justly and sought truth (Jeremiah 5:1).

The phrase “for their sakes” carries the weight of substitution. The many may be spared because of the few. That idea finds its fulfilment in the One Righteous Man, Jesus Christ, for whose sake the sins of many are pardoned (Romans 5:18–19).

The LORD’s readiness also corrects a common picture of God as eager to punish and reluctant to forgive. In this dialogue it is God who agrees at once and Abraham who hesitates, fearing to presume. The obstacle to Sodom’s preservation will not be any harshness in God but the absence of the righteous people who would have given mercy its ground. Judgment, when it comes, will be what Isaiah calls the LORD’s “strange work” (Isaiah 28:21).

wordNotes.term: וְנָשָׂאתִי לְכָל־הַמָּקוֹם (wenasaʾti lekhol-hammaqom) — I will spare all the place
wordNotes.explanation: The LORD answers with the same verb Abraham used in verse 24, nasaʾ, “lift” or “bear.” God takes up Abraham’s word and grants it. The verb is also used in Exodus 34:7 when the LORD proclaims himself as one who forgives (“bears”) iniquity, transgression, and sin.

wordNotes.term: בַּעֲבוּרָם (baʿavuram) — for their sakes
wordNotes.explanation: The preposition baʿavur means “on account of” or “for the sake of.” It recurs through the dialogue (vv. 29, 31, 32) and is used of the LORD blessing others on account of someone (26:24; 39:5). The righteous become the reason the whole city receives mercy.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham answered and said, Behold now, I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord, which am but dust and ashes:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Before pressing further, Abraham acknowledges his place. “Behold now, I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord, which am but dust and ashes.” He knows he has ventured something daring. He is a creature addressing his Creator, a sinner speaking to the holy Judge. His boldness does not rest on any standing of his own.

“Dust and ashes” is a vivid description of human frailty. Dust recalls the material from which God formed the first man (2:7) and the sentence pronounced after the fall: “dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return” (3:19). Ashes add the picture of what remains after burning, worthless and lifeless. Together the words confess that human beings have no life in themselves. Man is mortal, dependent wholly on God for breath and existence; immortality is not a natural possession but a gift God alone can give (1 Timothy 6:16; Romans 2:7). Job uses the same pair when he repents before God (Job 30:19; 42:6).

The humility is not a pretext. It is the condition that makes Abraham’s boldness acceptable. Those who approach God aware of their own nothingness can speak freely, because they do not claim merit. Jesus contrasted the Pharisee, who reminded God of his virtues, with the tax collector, who stood far off and said, “God be merciful to me a sinner” (Luke 18:13). It was the humble one who went home justified. Abraham’s greatness in prayer begins in his confession of littleness.

Abraham’s confession also clarifies the shape of his boldness. He does not argue from what he is, but from what God is. His own nature is dust; the Judge’s nature is righteousness. Every appeal in the dialogue rests on that second fact, which is why he can be humble and persistent at once.

wordNotes.term: עָפָר וָאֵפֶר (ʿafar waʾefer) — dust and ashes
wordNotes.explanation: The two words are close in sound, forming a rhyming pair that expresses lowliness and mortality. ʿAfar is the dust from which man was formed and to which he returns (2:7; 3:19); ʾefer is ash, often associated with mourning and humiliation (2 Samuel 13:19; Job 42:6). The pair confesses that human life is fragile and derived from God.

wordNotes.term: הוֹאַלְתִּי (hoʾalti) — I have taken upon me
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to undertake, venture, or resolve to do something, often with a sense of boldness or presumption (Deuteronomy 1:5; Judges 19:6). Abraham recognises that his speaking to God is a daring step. He repeats the expression in verse 31.

verses.bibleText: Peradventure there shall lack five of the fifty righteous: wilt thou destroy all the city for lack of five? And he said, If I find there forty and five, I will not destroy it.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abraham lowers the number with great care. He does not ask outright whether forty-five would be enough. Instead he frames the question around what would be missing: “Peradventure there shall lack five of the fifty righteous: wilt thou destroy all the city for lack of five?” Put that way, the request seems small. Would the Judge of all the earth really destroy a whole city because it fell five short?

The LORD’s reply is again immediate and generous: “If I find there forty and five, I will not destroy it.” He does not rebuke Abraham for persistence or accuse him of bargaining. Each concession shows a God who is more willing to show mercy than his servant had dared to expect. Jesus taught the same about prayer: the Father is ready to give good things to those who ask him (Luke 11:9–13), and persistence in asking is welcomed, not resented (Luke 18:1).

The shape of the request also reveals Abraham’s growing perception. He is learning, step by step, how far the mercy of God extends.

wordNotes.term: יַחְסְרוּן (yaḥserun) — there shall lack
wordNotes.explanation: The verb ḥaser means to be lacking, to fall short, or to be in want. It is used of the waters decreasing after the flood (8:3, 5) and in the confession “I shall not want” (Psalm 23:1). Abraham focuses on the small shortfall rather than the large remainder.

verses.bibleText: And he spake unto him yet again, and said, Peradventure there shall be forty found there. And he said, I will not do it for forty's sake.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he spake unto him yet again.” Abraham continues, now dropping by ten: “Peradventure there shall be forty found there.” His question grows shorter as his boldness and his awareness of presumption grow together. He no longer builds an argument; he simply names the number.

The LORD’s answer is equally brief: “I will not do it for forty’s sake.” The pattern is now established. Every time Abraham asks, God agrees. The repetition is part of the message. The text slows down so that the reader feels the steady patience of God, who hears request after request without impatience.

Abraham is not wearing down a reluctant deity. The narrator has already shown that the LORD chose to disclose his plan and left room for a different outcome (v. 21). Each petition simply uncovers more of the mercy that was there from the start, the way successive steps down a stair reveal a deeper floor than the first glance suggested.

wordNotes.term: וַיֹּסֶף עוֹד (wayyosef ʿod) — and he spake yet again
wordNotes.explanation: The verb yasaf, “to add” or “do again,” combined with ʿod, “still,” marks persistent repetition. The same construction describes repeated actions throughout narrative (8:12; 38:5). Abraham keeps adding his requests.

verses.bibleText: And he said unto him, Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak: Peradventure there shall thirty be found there. And he said, I will not do it, if I find thirty there.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Before the next step Abraham pauses to guard against offence: “Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak.” He is conscious that his persistence could seem like presumption. A servant who pressed a king again and again might provoke anger, and Abraham knows he is standing before One far greater than any king. His words recall the reverent caution of Gideon, who used the same plea when asking for another sign (Judges 6:39).

Then he names the number: “Peradventure there shall thirty be found there.” The jump is now larger, from forty to thirty. Abraham seems to sense that the number of righteous in Sodom may be very small. The LORD answers once more: “I will not do it, if I find thirty there.”

The LORD does not grow angry. His patience matches his promise in Exodus 34:6, “merciful and gracious, longsuffering.” Abraham’s fear of offending God is a mark of reverence, and God’s gentle reply shows that such reverent boldness pleases him. Those who know God best are often those most aware of his majesty and at the same time most free to ask.

The progression also exposes something about Sodom. Abraham’s numbers fall because his confidence in the city falls. He knows Lot’s situation and has seen the city’s king and its ways (14:17–24). Every lower figure is an unspoken admission that righteousness there has become scarce. Yet he continues to ask, because the character of the Judge gives him hope even when the condition of the city does not. Intercession often works this way: the one who prays sees the darkness plainly and still appeals to the light of God’s mercy.

wordNotes.term: אַל־נָא יִחַר לַאדֹנָי (ʾal-naʾ yiḥar laʾdonay) — Oh let not the Lord be angry
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “let it not burn to the Lord,” since anger in Hebrew is often pictured as heat or burning (Exodus 32:10–11). Abraham’s request is polite and reverent, asking pardon in advance. Gideon uses the identical phrase in Judges 6:39.

verses.bibleText: And he said, Behold now, I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord: Peradventure there shall be twenty found there. And he said, I will not destroy it for twenty's sake.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abraham repeats his earlier confession of daring: “Behold now, I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord.” The words recall verse 27, though he now omits “dust and ashes.” The repetition shows that his humility has not been lost amid his growing boldness.

He asks about twenty, and the LORD replies: “I will not destroy it for twenty’s sake.” Each step down widens the scope of God’s mercy. Twenty righteous would preserve a whole city. The arithmetic of grace runs against human expectation. Few can bring blessing to many, a truth the New Testament carries into the image of salt and light in the world (Matthew 5:13–14).

Abraham’s caution does not hinder his persistence; the two belong together in the kind of prayer God honours, the kind that knows both who God is and how great the need is.

wordNotes.term: לְדַבֵּר אֶל־אֲדֹנָי (ledabber ʾel-ʾadonay) — to speak unto the Lord
wordNotes.explanation: Abraham addresses God as ʾAdonay, Lord or Master, a title expressing submission and reverence. The narrator uses the covenant name YHWH, but Abraham speaks as a servant to his sovereign (Psalm 123:2; Malachi 1:6).

verses.bibleText: And he said, Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak yet but this once: Peradventure ten shall be found there. And he said, I will not destroy it for ten's sake.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak yet but this once.” Abraham signals that this is his final request. He has gone as far as he dares. “Peradventure ten shall be found there.” And the LORD answers: “I will not destroy it for ten’s sake.”

Why does Abraham stop at ten? The text does not say, but several reasons fit the story. Ten is the smallest number that can still be called a community. Fewer than ten could be rescued individually, as Lot and his daughters eventually were, without sparing the whole city. Abraham may also have counted Lot’s household: Lot, his wife, two unmarried daughters, married daughters and sons-in-law (19:12–14). If even Lot’s family had been faithful, the number might have been reached. Later Jewish practice set ten as the minimum number for communal prayer, reflecting the same sense that ten form a congregation.

The outcome of the next chapter shows that not even ten were found. Sodom had become so corrupt that the whole population, “both old and young, all the people from every quarter,” joined in the assault on the angels (19:4). Yet Abraham’s prayer was not wasted. The Lord delivered Lot and his daughters, and the narrator explains why: “God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow” (19:29). The answer exceeded the request in its own way. Abraham had asked that the city be spared for the righteous; God rescued the righteous from the city.

The dialogue also shows that intercession has limits. Abraham did not ask God to spare Sodom unconditionally. He recognised that there is a point beyond which mercy toward the wicked would only confirm them in wickedness. Ezekiel later declared that even Noah, Daniel, and Job could save only themselves if a land persisted in rebellion (Ezekiel 14:14). Probation can close.

Abraham’s plea anticipates a greater intercession. He stood before God for a guilty city on the basis of a righteous few. Christ stands before the Father for guilty humanity on the basis of his own perfect righteousness. He “ever liveth to make intercession” for those who come to God by him (Hebrews 7:25). Where Abraham could find no ten righteous in Sodom, Christ became the one Righteous for the many (1 Peter 3:18).

wordNotes.term: אַךְ־הַפַּעַם (ʾakh-happaʿam) — yet but this once
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase means “only this time,” signalling a last request. Gideon uses it with the same sense when asking for a final sign (Judges 6:39), and Samson in his last prayer (Judges 16:28). Abraham recognises the boundary of reverent persistence.

wordNotes.term: עֲשָׂרָה (ʿasarah) — ten
wordNotes.explanation: Ten often represents a complete or minimal group in Scripture: ten commandments (Exodus 34:28), ten men of a city as witnesses (Ruth 4:2), ten virgins in the parable (Matthew 25:1). Here it marks the smallest righteous community for whose sake God would spare a city.

verses.bibleText: And the LORD went his way, as soon as he had left communing with Abraham: and Abraham returned unto his place.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the LORD went his way, as soon as he had left communing with Abraham.” The conversation ends at God’s initiative. Abraham had said he would speak only once more, and when he finishes, the LORD departs. God remained sovereign throughout the dialogue. He welcomed Abraham’s pleading and granted every request, but the decision about Sodom remained his.

“And Abraham returned unto his place.” He goes back to Mamre, to his tent and his ordinary life. He does not follow the angels down to Sodom or try to intervene in person. Having laid his concern before God, he leaves the matter with the Judge of all the earth. The next morning he will rise early, return to the place where he had stood before the LORD, and look toward the smoking plain (19:27–28). He will see that God has acted, and he will know that the Judge has done right.

This closing verse carries a lesson about prayer. True intercession does not end in anxiety or in grasping control. It ends in trust. Abraham pleaded boldly, then rested. Paul exhorts believers to make their requests known to God with thanksgiving, and promises that the peace of God will guard their hearts (Philippians 4:6–7).

The whole chapter reveals a God who draws near to his friend, eats at his table, shares his counsel, and listens to his pleas. It also reveals the kind of person God can trust with his secrets: one who welcomes strangers, believes promises, teaches righteousness, and cares for the lost. Abraham’s intercession points beyond itself to Christ, our High Priest in the heavenly sanctuary, who pleads for sinners and who will one day return to gather his people and bring final justice to the earth (Hebrews 9:24, 28).
