wordNotes.term: כַּאֲשֶׁר כִּלָּה לְדַבֵּר (kaʾasher killah ledabber) — as soon as he had left communing
wordNotes.explanation: The verb kalah in this form means to finish or bring to completion. The same expression closes other divine conversations: God “left off talking” with Abraham in 17:22, and finished speaking with Moses on Sinai (Exodus 31:18). The conversation reached its end by God’s decision.

wordNotes.term: שָׁב לִמְקֹמוֹ (shav limqomo) — returned unto his place
wordNotes.explanation: “His place” is Abraham’s dwelling at Mamre. The word maqom also appears in 19:27, where Abraham returns to “the place where he stood before the LORD.” Maqom can denote a place of worship or encounter with God (22:3; 28:11). Abraham’s return frames the episode as a meeting in a particular place and time.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What does it reveal about God that he chooses to sit at a man’s table before announcing both a birth and a judgment?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: The LORD draws near to his friends in fellowship, keeps promises that exceed human possibility, and shares his just purposes with those he calls to intercede for others.
discussionQuestions: How does Abraham’s welcome to strangers prepare him to recognize the LORD among them?
Why does the LORD address Sarah’s laughter through Abraham, and what does his final word to her accomplish?
What connection does verse 19 draw between Abraham’s election and the instruction of his household?
What does Abraham’s prayer assume about God’s character, and how does God’s answer confirm it?
Why might Abraham have stopped at ten, and what does chapter 19 show about God’s mercy beyond the request?
commonMisunderstandings: The three visitors are not a picture of the three persons of the Godhead; the text identifies one as the LORD and the other two as angels (19:1).
“I will go down now, and see” does not mean God lacked knowledge; it shows that his judgments are investigated and open to view before they are carried out.
Abraham’s bargaining does not change God’s mind about justice; it draws out the mercy already in God’s heart.
Sarah’s rebuke is not rejection; the same word that exposed her laughter promised her a son.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep together God’s nearness and his majesty: the guest who eats under the tree is the Judge of all the earth, and the friend who argues for Sodom confesses that he is dust and ashes.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: The God who visited Abraham’s tent still comes near to those who will receive him, still keeps his impossible promises, and still invites his people to stand before him on behalf of a world under judgment.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: The Judge of all the earth is also the God who comes near in grace, keeps his promises, and delights to show mercy for the sake of the righteous.
flow: God draws near to human beings and seeks fellowship with them.
His promises rest on his power, not on our ability to believe them easily.
He sees sin truly and judges it justly after full investigation.
He is willing to spare the guilty for the sake of the righteous, a mercy fulfilled in Christ the Righteous One.
We are invited to receive that mercy and to plead for others while probation lasts.
simpleIllustrations: A traveller who stops at an unknown house expecting a cup of water and finds a banquet prepared shows how God’s gifts outrun our requests.
A lawyer who argues a case by appealing to the judge’s own known fairness pictures Abraham resting his prayer on God’s character.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you trust the God for whom nothing is too hard, and join Abraham in pleading for those who are near judgment?
cautions: Do not present Sodom’s destruction as unending torment; Scripture describes it as an overthrow that turned the cities to ashes.
Do not use Sarah’s doubt to shame struggling believers; the LORD corrected her and still kept his word.
Do not imply that intercession earns salvation for others apart from their own response to God.

reflectionQuestions: Am I ready to welcome interruptions and strangers as opportunities God may use, as Abraham did in the heat of the day?
Where have I laughed inwardly at a promise of God because my circumstances seemed to make it impossible?
How am I passing on “the way of the LORD” to the people in my household and care?
When I think about God’s judgments, do I rest on the conviction that the Judge of all the earth will do right?
For whom should I be standing before the LORD in persistent, humble prayer this week?
